facts.claim: Hinton, Vinyals and Dean (2015) train a small model on the odds a large model gives each answer, used as “soft targets”, raising the large model’s temperature until those odds are spread out enough.
The same paper notes that when the soft targets are spread out, each training example gives much more information than the single right answer does.
FrugalGPT is an LLM cascade that learns which combinations of models to use for different queries; its authors report it can match the best single model (GPT-4) with up to 98% cost reduction.
RouteLLM trains routers that pick between a stronger and a weaker model for each query; its authors report cutting costs by more than half in some cases without losing response quality.

As of 30 October 2026, Anthropic lists Claude Haiku 4.5 at $1 per million input tokens and $5 per million output tokens, and Claude Opus 4.5 at $5 and $25: that small model costs a fifth as much per token, in and out. Newer pairs on the same list are priced differently, so the ratio depends on the two models you compare.

Kaplan et al. (2020) estimate that running a transformer language model on one token takes roughly 2 operations per weight, a multiply and an add, plus a smaller part that grows with the text it reads.

Stanton et al. (2021) find a surprisingly large gap often remains between a distilled student’s odds and its teacher’s, even when the student could match exactly, and that matching the teacher more closely does not always make the student better on new data.

Echterhoff et al. (2024) find that when a large language model is updated to a newer version, tasks trained on it the same way show “negative flips”: questions the old version got right that the new one gets wrong.

Ding et al. (2024) route each question to a small or a large model by how hard it is predicted to be, and report up to 40% fewer calls to the large model with no drop in response quality, in their tests.
